pos: n. (proper name; a station on the southern border of Canaan)
etymology: Hebrew Chatsar 'Addar, village of Addar, from chatser, enclosure, village, and 'addar, glorious, wide.
biblical_def: Hazaraddar is a point on the southern border of the land as the LORD drew it for Moses: “And your border shall turn from the south to the ascent of Akrabbim, and pass on to Zin: and the going forth thereof shall be from the south to Kadeshbarnea, and shall go on to Hazaraddar, and pass on to Azmon” (Numbers 34:4). Joshua, tracing the same line as the border of Judah, gives it in the shorter form Adar: the border “passed along to Hezron, and went up to Adar, and fetched a compass to Karkaa” (Joshua 15:3). It is not the month Adar of the book of Esther. The value of the name lies in the chapter that contains it. Before Israel had crossed the Jordan, God gave them a surveyed land with fixed edges, “the land that shall fall unto you for an inheritance, even the land of Canaan with the coasts thereof” (Numbers 34:2). The promise was specific enough to be walked out stake by stake, and Hazaraddar was one of the stakes.

pos: n. (proper name; a town of Judah taken by the Philistines under Ahaz)
etymology: Hebrew Gimzo, perhaps place of sycamores, from shiqmah, sycamore, by a contracted form; the meaning is uncertain.
biblical_def: Gimzo is a town of the Judean lowland lost to the Philistines in the reign of Ahaz: “The Philistines also had invaded the cities of the low country, and of the south of Judah, and had taken Bethshemesh, and Ajalon, and Gederoth, and Shocho with the villages thereof, and Timnah with the villages thereof, Gimzo also and the villages thereof: and they dwelt there” (2 Chronicles 28:18). The Chronicler gives the reason in the next verse: “For the LORD brought Judah low because of Ahaz king of Israel; for he made Judah naked, and transgressed sore against the LORD” (2 Chronicles 28:19). Ahaz had shut the doors of the temple, sacrificed his sons in the fire, and sought help from Assyria rather than from God. The loss of the lowland towns was not a mere military setback; it was the LORD stripping a faithless king. Gimzo, last in the list, marks how far the Philistine tide came inland when Judah's king had made the nation naked before its God.

etymology: Hebrew Gur Ba'al, dwelling of Baal, from gur, to sojourn, dwell, and ba'al.
biblical_def: Gurbaal is named once, in the account of Uzziah's wars: “And God helped him against the Philistines, and against the Arabians that dwelt in Gurbaal, and the Mehunims” (2 Chronicles 26:7). Its location is unknown, though it lay somewhere on Judah's southern or eastern desert edge where Arabian tribes ranged. The Chronicler's emphasis falls on the words God helped him. Uzziah's early reign is a study in blessing: “he sought God in the days of Zechariah, who had understanding in the visions of God: and as long as he sought the LORD, God made him to prosper” (2 Chronicles 26:5). His victories, his towers, his cisterns and his engines of war all flowed from that. The same chapter records his fall, when his heart was lifted up and he went into the temple to burn incense, and was smitten with leprosy until the day of his death. Gurbaal belongs to the years when he still sought the LORD.

pos: n. (proper name; the ascent by Ibleam where Ahaziah of Judah was wounded)
etymology: Hebrew Gur, whelp or sojourning, from gur, a lion's whelp, or the verb to sojourn.
biblical_def: Gur is the ascent where Jehu's men overtook Ahaziah king of Judah: “But when Ahaziah the king of Judah saw this, he fled by the way of the garden house. And Jehu followed after him, and said, Smite him also in the chariot. And they did so at the going up to Gur, which is by Ibleam. And he fled to Megiddo, and died there” (2 Kings 9:27). Moments before, Jehu had shot Jehoram of Israel through the heart and had his body cast into the plot of Naboth's field, “according to the word of the LORD” (2 Kings 9:26). Ahaziah died because he was there: the son of Athaliah, grandson of Ahab, visiting his uncle in Jezreel, joined to the house the LORD had sentenced. Gur marks the place where kinship with Ahab's house became fatal to a king of David's line. His servants carried him to Jerusalem and buried him with his fathers, but his mother Athaliah would answer his death by murdering the royal seed.

pos: n. (proper name; a place near Gibeon where Joab's pursuit of Abner ended)
etymology: Hebrew Giach, a gushing forth, from giach, to burst forth, as a spring.
biblical_def: Giah is named in the account of the civil war between David's house and Saul's: “Joab also and Abishai pursued after Abner: and the sun went down when they were come to the hill of Ammah, that lieth before Giah by the way of the wilderness of Gibeon” (2 Samuel 2:24). Abner had just killed Asahel, Joab's brother, who would not turn aside from chasing him. At sunset by Giah, the Benjamites rallied on a hilltop, and Abner called down a question that still rings: “Shall the sword devour for ever? knowest thou not that it will be bitterness in the latter end? how long shall it be then, ere thou bid the people return from following their brethren?” (2 Samuel 2:26). Joab blew the trumpet and the pursuit ended. Giah, a gushing spring, is the place where brothers stopped shedding brothers' blood for one night, though Joab did not forget Asahel and later murdered Abner in the gate of Hebron.

pos: n. (proper name; a Canaanite town in Asher's territory never driven out)
biblical_def: Helbah is one of the towns the tribe of Asher failed to take: “Neither did Asher drive out the inhabitants of Accho, nor the inhabitants of Zidon, nor of Ahlab, nor of Achzib, nor of Helbah, nor of Aphik, nor of Rehob” (Judges 1:31). The next verse makes Asher's situation worse than that of the other tribes: “But the Asherites dwelt among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land: for they did not drive them out” (Judges 1:32). Elsewhere the Canaanites dwelt among Israel; here Israel dwelt among the Canaanites, a minority in its own inheritance. Helbah's name, fatness, suits the rich coastal plain north of Carmel, and that richness may explain the failure: a fertile land well held by its people was costly to take, and easy to share. Judges opens with this list so that the reader will understand everything that follows. The book's cycles of idolatry begin in towns like Helbah, left standing beside Israel's tents.

pos: n. (proper name; the battlefield beyond Jordan where David defeated the Syrians)
etymology: Hebrew Cheylam, perhaps stronghold or their army, from chayil, strength, army.
biblical_def: Helam is the place east of the Jordan where David broke the Syrian coalition that came to help Ammon. After their first defeat before Joab, the Syrians regrouped: “And when the Syrians saw that they were smitten before Israel, they gathered themselves together” (2 Samuel 10:15). Hadarezer sent for the Syrians beyond the Euphrates, and they came to Helam. “And when it was told David, he gathered all Israel together, and passed over Jordan, and came to Helam. And the Syrians set themselves in array against David, and fought with him” (2 Samuel 10:17). The result was decisive: David slew the men of seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen, and smote Shobach the captain of their host. “And when all the kings that were servants to Hadarezer saw that they were smitten before Israel, they made peace with Israel, and served them” (2 Samuel 10:19). Helam was the battle that brought Syria under David and fulfilled the promise of rest from his enemies round about.

pos: n. (proper name; the villages of the Avims on the southern coast before the Philistines)
etymology: Hebrew Chatserim, villages or enclosures, plural of chatser, court, unwalled settlement.
biblical_def: Hazerim is named in Moses' historical notes on the peoples who held lands before Israel: “And the Avims which dwelt in Hazerim, even unto Azzah, the Caphtorims, which came forth out of Caphtor, destroyed them, and dwelt in their stead” (Deuteronomy 2:23). The word is the ordinary Hebrew plural for unwalled villages, and the King James translators kept it as a name; it describes the settlements of the Avims along the coast as far as Azzah, that is, Gaza. The Caphtorims, from Caphtor, the people later known as the Philistines, dispossessed them. Moses sets this note beside the others in Deuteronomy 2, how Esau took Seir from the Horims and Moab and Ammon took their lands from the Emims and Zamzummims, to make one point: the LORD apportions lands to the nations and removes peoples from them. If He did so for Esau and Lot and the Caphtorims, He would surely do so for Israel.

biblical_def: Kibzaim is one of the four cities of Ephraim given to the Kohathite Levites: “And Kibzaim with her suburbs, and Bethhoron with her suburbs; four cities” (Joshua 21:22). The parallel list in Chronicles gives Jokmeam in its place: “And Jokmeam with her suburbs, and Bethhoron with her suburbs” (1 Chronicles 6:68), and the two names are generally taken as the same town. The Kohathites who were not priests “had the cities of their lot out of the tribe of Ephraim” (Joshua 21:20), beginning with Shechem, a city of refuge, and Gezer. The Levites received no tribal territory, but forty-eight cities scattered through all Israel, so that the teachers of the law lived among every tribe. Kibzaim's name, a double gathering, is apt for a Levitical town, a place where a scattered tribe was gathered so that it could be scattered again in service.

pos: n. (proper name; a valley on the border of Zebulun and Asher)
etymology: Hebrew Yiphtach-'el, God opens, from pathach, to open, and 'el, God; the same verb as in the name Jephthah.
biblical_def: The valley of Jiphthahel marks the border between Zebulun and Asher. In the lot of Zebulun, “the border compasseth it on the north side to Hannathon: and the outgoings thereof are in the valley of Jiphthahel” (Joshua 19:14). In the lot of Asher the same valley appears from the other side: the border “reacheth to Zebulun, and to the valley of Jiphthahel toward the north side of Bethemek, and Neiel, and goeth out to Cabul on the left hand” (Joshua 19:27). Two tribes' lots meet in one valley, and the agreement of the two descriptions is a small mark of a single, coherent survey. The name, God opens, uses the verb of Jephthah's name and of the opening of wombs, of eyes, and of the windows of heaven. A border valley called God opens is a fitting boundary in a land given by lot, where each tribe received what God opened to it. The chapter ends, “This is the inheritance of the children of Zebulun according to their families” (Joshua 19:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Jiphthahel is a Hebrew proper name and has no entry in Webster's dictionary of the English language.
webster_full: Jiphthahel is a Hebrew proper name; Webster's 1828 dictionary treats common English words and does not define it.
The name appears twice, in Joshua 19:14 and 19:27.
It was a valley on the border of Zebulun and Asher.
Zebulun's border went out in it on the north.
Asher's border reached it toward Beth-emek.

corruption_summary: The boundary lists of Joshua are called artificial compositions; their cross-agreement shows a single coherent survey.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical scholarship often treats Joshua's boundary lists as idealised constructions from a later age. Their internal agreement, Zebulun's north border and Asher's south border meeting in the same valley, is the mark of a real survey of a real land.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the lot is the LORD's. Each tribe's portion was opened to it by God, and the border valley carries that confession in its name.
